newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu says Hutus out of Zaire, UN force shapes up.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu says Hutus out of Zaire, UN force shapes up.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko has thrown his weight behind moves to send home more than a million Hutu refugees caught at the centre of warfare in east Zaire.
Canada stepped forward on Tuesday to lead a planned multinational force to secure food aid and passage for the refugees scattered by three weeks of violence in east Zaire.

But judging by the firm statement by Mobutu -- until now the protector of Hutus who fear revenge at home for a massacre of Tutsis -- the intervention force's main task will be providing safe conduct back to Rwanda for the refugees.
"The refugees are the source of many problems," Mobutu told a television interviewer in France where he is convalescing after cancer surgery.
"So everyone should go home and each government take the responsibility of looking after its citizens," he said in the interview broadcast on Tuesday.
Most of the Hutus are Rwandans who fled after the 1994 massacre of up to a million Tutsis or their sympathisers. But some are Burundians who fled massacres in their own homeland.

The governments of Rwanda and Burundi, both led by Tutsis, as well as the Zaire authorities, want the Hutus back in their countries. So do ethnic Tutsi rebels who have seized Zaire's two eastern provinces where refugee camps were located.
Many of the refugees also say they want to go home but that they are being prevented by armed Hutu hardliners, most of them former Rwandan soldiers who led the 1994 genocide.

Hardline Hutus, apparently using refugees as human shields, are battling ethnic Tutsis around Mugunga camp near Goma. The situation in the camp has been unclear since the Tutsis defeated the Zaire army in recent fighting.
Most of 1.2 million camp refugees and hundreds of thousands of Zairean villagers fled into the jungle where aid workers say thousands could die of hunger or disease.
Canada said on Tuesday it had agreed to lead a multinational military force to take food, water and other aid to the refugees but details of the operation were still being worked out.

Canada told officials at the United Nations it needs more than 10,000 troops for the operation, which it expects to last four to six months, U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said. After that time any mission, if needed, would be under a U.N. flag.

Among the countries that have expressed a willingness to join the force are France, Spain, Italy, South Africa, Ethiopia and Mali. Still key to the operation are anticipated responses from the United States and Britain before the U.N. Security Council formally approves the operation.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros Ghali said in Rome that he expected more than 12 countries to participate.

France has been pushing for a multinational force to go into Zaire but it is not trusted by the Rwanda government, which accuses Paris of helping Hutu killers escape during a similar intervention by French troops in 1994.
Major powers, notably the United States and Britain, also reacted coolly to the French idea but have lately warmed up to some form of participation.
How the force goes in, and notably where the French are stationed, would have to take account of the strong views of both Rwanda and Zaire whose consent is key, diplomats say.

Aid sources in the Zaire capital said that the military operation would most likely be based in Zaire and go along with Zaire's demand for a protected east-west corridor along which the refugees could return home.

U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien who is negotiating a mandate for the intervention force, returned to Kinshasa on Tuesday for talks with Zaire authorities, continuing a shuttle diplomacy between Zaire and Rwanda.
